questions.q: Define 'long-term sources of finance' as per NCERT classification and give two examples.
questions.a: Long-term sources provide funds for a period exceeding 5 years. Examples: issue of equity shares, issue of debentures, long-term loans from financial institutions. A wrong answer (e.g., "public deposits" or "trade credit") reveals the student confuses medium-term (1-5 years) with long-term (>5 years) or ignores the 5-year threshold.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why retained earnings are classified as 'owner's funds' but not as 'borrowed funds', even though both are internal to the company.
questions.a: Retained earnings are owner's funds because they belong to shareholders (residual claim), carry no repayment obligation, no fixed interest/dividend commitment, and strengthen the ownership base. Borrowed funds create a legal liability to repay principal + interest regardless of profit. A wrong answer focusing only on "internal source" misses the ownership vs. creditor distinction — a classic confusion between *source of generation* (internal/external) and *ownership basis* (owner/borrowed).

questions.q: Classify the following sources into the 2×3 matrix (Period: Long/Medium/Short × Ownership: Owner's/Borrowed): (a) Commercial Paper, (b) Preference Shares, (c) Lease Financing, (d) Public Deposits (3-year maturity), (e) Trade Credit.
questions.a: (a) Short-term, Borrowed; (b) Long-term, Owner's; (c) Medium-term, Borrowed; (d) Medium-term, Borrowed; (e) Short-term, Borrowed. A wrong classification (e.g., putting Preference Shares as Borrowed because of fixed dividend, or Lease Financing as Owner's because lessee uses the asset) reveals misunderstanding of the *legal nature* of the instrument: preference shares are equity (ownership) despite fixed dividend; lease is a rental contract (borrowed usage right), not ownership transfer.

questions.q: A company needs ₹10 crore for machinery (useful life 10 years) and ₹2 crore for seasonal inventory (cycle 4 months). Analyze why using a single source (e.g., 1-year bank loan) for both would violate the principle of maturity matching. Use period basis classification in your answer.
questions.a: Machinery requires long-term funds (>5 years) because the asset generates returns over 10 years; a 1-year loan creates refinancing risk and liquidity crunch when the loan matures but the asset isn't liquidated. Seasonal inventory needs short-term funds (≤1 year) because it converts to cash in 4 months; a long-term loan would incur unnecessary interest cost during idle periods. Maturity matching aligns asset life with liability maturity. A wrong answer ignoring the asset-liability duration mismatch shows inability to apply period classification to real financing decisions.

questions.q: Evaluate: "For a startup wanting to avoid dilution of control and having unstable early earnings, debentures are a better source than equity shares." Justify using ownership basis and risk concepts.
questions.a: The statement is **flawed**. While debentures avoid voting dilution (ownership basis: borrowed funds, no control), they impose fixed interest obligation regardless of earnings — dangerous for a startup with unstable income (high financial risk). Equity shares dilute control but have no compulsory dividend (ownership basis: owner's funds, residual claim), aligning payouts with ability to pay. Better: mix both or use convertible debentures. A wrong answer focusing only on "no dilution" ignores the risk dimension of ownership classification — a senior secondary error.

questions.q: Create a financing plan for a medium-sized textile manufacturer needing ₹25 crore for: (i) new weaving plant (15-year life), (ii) cotton stock for 6 months, (iii) ERP software (3-year useful life). Specify one source for each, classify by period & ownership, and defend your choices.
questions.a: (i) Plant: 10-year debentures (Long-term, Borrowed) — matches asset life, tax-deductible interest. (ii) Cotton stock: Trade credit (Short-term, Borrowed) — self-liquidating, no asset charge. (iii) ERP: Lease financing (Medium-term, Borrowed) — avoids obsolescence risk, lower upfront cash. Good answer shows each source's period matches asset life, ownership choice balances control/cost/risk. Poor answer uses same source for all or mismatches periods (e.g., trade credit for plant).

What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can independently classify any given source of finance (e.g., commercial paper, lease financing, equity shares) by both period and ownership basis, and justify the classification with reference to maturity, repayment obligation, control implications, and cost structure.
